TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

       Pursuant to SOAH Order No. 32 issued in this docket, John D. Harkey, Jr., The Mason
Trust, Black Jack Ranch Trust, and Harkey Ranch Enterprises, Inc. (together, “Harkey Ranch”)
timely file this Initial Brief and respectfully shows as follows:

                   I.        INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT

       On March 26, 2026, Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC ("Oncor") and LCRA
Transmission Service Corporation ("LCRA") (collectively, “Applicants”) jointly filed an
application to amend their certificates of convenience and necessity (“CCN”) for the construction
of a new 765-kV transmission line between the Bell County East Switch and the Big Hill
Substation (the “Project”) as part of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan implementation.1 The
Project, wherever ultimately sited, will span over 200 miles across multiple counties located in the
heart of Texas.2

       Harkey Ranch supports approval of Route 894, the route selected by Oncor Electric
Delivery Company LLC ("Oncor") and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation ("LCRA")

       1
           Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 1.
       2
           Id. at Bates 9.

 (collectively, “Applicants”) as the route that best meets the applicable routing criteria under the
Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”)3 and the Public Utility Commission of Texas’ (“PUCT”
or “Commission”) Substantive Rules. Alternatively, Harkey Ranch does not oppose Route 487, as
recommended by Commission Staff. Harkey Ranch strongly opposes Route Cherokee G ("CCG"),
as well as any route or route modification that includes either Link L1 or Link K42.

        Harkey Ranch is located in southern McCulloch and northern Mason Counties. The Ranch
property includes parcels identified by Oncor as parcel numbers 974, 975, 976, and 977.4 Link L1
runs through a major portion of the historic portion of the Ranch which includes sensitive
geological features and habitat restoration areas as well the Ranch operation center; the property
also abuts proposed Link K42.5

        The Harkey Ranch was founded in 1898 and has been under continuous family stewardship
for more than 125 years.6 It is recognized as a Texas Century Ranch / Family Land Heritage
Ranch.7 The Ranch includes cattle operations, wildlife management and habitat conservation,
family, staff, and visitor facilities, business and operational centers, water and irrigation
infrastructure, aviation facilities, and significant historical, archeological, cultural, geological, and
aesthetic resources.8 Siting the Project along a route that includes links L1 and K42 would place a
new high-voltage corridor in the middle of a heavily improved and operationally critical portion
of the Harkey Ranch, would result in irreparable habitat fragmentation and cause significant
damage and disruption to the Ranch and its operations.9

        For the reasons discussed herein, Harkey Ranch urges the Honorable SOAH
Administrative Law Judges, and ultimately, the PUCT Commissioners, to select Route 894 or
another alternative route that does not utilize links L1 and K42.

                                                II.      ARGUMENT

    A. After balancing all factors specified by statute and PUCT rules, Route 894 best
       satisfies the routing criteria set forth in PURA and in Commission rules.

        1.      Factors Required to be Considered

         PURA § 37.056(c) specifies particular factors the Commission must consider when
granting or denying a CCN. The Commission is directed to consider the adequacy of existing
service, the need for additional service, the effect of granting the certificate on the applicant and
other utilities serving the proximate area, and other factors including community values,
recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, and environmental integrity.
Additionally, the Commission’s Substantive Rules at 16 Tex. Admin. Code (“TAC”) §
25.101(b)(3)(B) articulate with more specificity required consideration of engineering constraints,
costs, use or paralleling of existing compatible rights-of-way, paralleling of apparent property
boundaries or other natural or cultural features, moderation of impact on the affected community
and landowners, and the Commission’s policy of prudent avoidance.

        2. The Route best balancing the factors set out in statute and rule should be selected.

        Neither statute nor rule direct any single metric be controlling in the selection of a route on
which a transmission line will be placed. Nor does the Legislature assign values for any of the
designated factors to be weighed against each other. Rather, the Commission is called to evaluate
and weigh the routing criteria holistically. As former Chairman Barry Smitherman testified, “It’s
not a math question. It’s a balancing of factors.”10

        In recommending Route 894, the record evidence shows that the Applicants assessed the
alternatives in just that way.11

        3. Application and Assessment of Routing Criteria

        With their application, Applicants filed 122 alternative routes.12 As this matter has

for final selection. Routes 296, 392, 410, 487, 572, 891, 894, and RFI Route Cherokee G/CCG
each have their advocates.13 Given the significance of those routes and the attention they received
over the course of the Hearing on the Merits, it is reasonable to focus primarily on the comparative
performance of those Routes of Interest. For ease of reference, a table consisting of the measurable
routing data associated with each of the Routes of Interest is attached hereto as Attachment 1.14
For the reasons discussed below, Route 894 best meets the requirements established by PURA and
the PUCT Substantive Rules. Route 487 is an acceptable alternative.

                   a.           Route 894

        Route 894, recommended by Applicants as the “best meets” route, consists of links A0-
A1-A2-B1-B21-C4-D12-C5-E52-F1-F31-F32-F20-F23-G72-G73-G82-G13-G51-G52-H1-H41-

894 would be 223.7 miles long,16 has an estimated cost of $1,680,919,000,17 and has 85 habitable
structures within 500 feet of its centerline.18 Despite recommending Route 487, Commission
Staff’s expert witness, Mr. Poole, testified that he considers Route 894 “a very good route.”19

        By comparison, Route CCG costs approximately $73.69 million more, is approximately
9.02 miles longer, has 20 more habitable structures, has 55 more stream crossings, has six more
recorded cultural resources within 1,000 feet, has about 8.45 more miles of high
archeological/historical site potential, and has 24 more FM/county/street crossings.20 At the
Hearing on the Merits, Mr. Poole acknowledged in his testimony that Route 894 has 20 fewer
habitable structures than CCG, that CCG is much longer than Route 894, and that the additional

CCG’s sponsor, testified that she did not consider total project costs in her recommendations,
acknowledging that that only 15 of the 122 filed routes have a total project cost greater than CCG,
making it one of the most expensive of the routes filed by the Applicants.22

        CCG also presents a critical environmental concern as it crosses an environmentally
sensitive stream segment.23 With regard to that segment, Mr. Poole testified that CCG crosses near
an existing AEP line at the San Saba River and that, if a flood could knock out a tower, locating
the proposed line next to an existing transmission line at that crossing creates the risk that an event
damaging both lines could create a potential single point of failure.24

        On balance, the record developed in this matter shows that Route 894 best addresses the
applicable routing criteria. Some of the criteria which received the closest scrutiny in the Hearing
are reviewed below.

      i.           Community Values, Prudent Avoidance, Habitable Structures
        Evaluation of route selection for a transmission line such as the one at issue in this
proceeding requires consideration of values and resources essential to a local community.25 Under
16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), a transmission line must be routed to the extent reasonable to moderate
the impact on the affected community and landowners unless grid reliability and security dictate
otherwise. It follows, then, that the route selected should minimize disruption to land use, industry,
and the local residents and their way of life.

        Route 894 best serves community values and adheres to the Commission’s policy of
prudent avoidance because it minimizes direct residential exposure. Route 894 has only 85
habitable structures within 500 feet of the route centerline, which is the fewest of the eight Routes
of Interest.26 By comparison, Route 894 includes 11 fewer habitable structures than Route 487, 20
fewer than Route 296 and CCG, 22 fewer than Route 572, 23 fewer than Route 891, and 51 fewer

comparatively low, and maintaining meaningful use of compatible rights-of-way and property

        Additionally, the record establishes that schools are considered habitable structures which
present public sensitivities that should be avoided when routing a transmission line.29 Florence
Elementary School, situated within the path of Link F34 was the only school identified within 500
feet in Applicants’ application materials.30 Route 894 does not include Link F34.31

     ii.           Recreational and Park Areas
        Route 894 crosses no park or recreational area, has no park or recreational area within
1,000 feet, and has no right-of-way within the foreground visual zone of parks or recreational
areas.32 That is the best possible performance with regard to the measurable routing criteria that
address this factor. That performance distinguishes Route 894 from the two lower cost Routes of
Interest, Routes 487 and 891. Route 487 has one park or recreational area within 1,000 feet and
4.25 miles of park visual-zone impact.33 Route 891 also has one park or recreational area within
1,000 feet and 1.63 miles of park visual-zone impact.34 Routes of Interest 296, 392, and 410 have
no parks within 1,000 feet, but each has some park visual-zone impact.35 Route 894 avoids those
impacts entirely.
     iii.          Historical and aesthetic values
        Route 894 performs well with regard to historical and aesthetic values criteria, as compared
to the other Routes of Interest. It crosses only two recorded cultural resource sites, tied for the best
result among the eight Routes of Interest.36 Further, Route 894 has only 12 recorded cultural

Route 894 also has 54.34 miles of high archeological/historical site potential, materially lower than

        Harkey Ranch contains Native American archeological features and artifact areas, a
designated pioneer cemetery, granite outcroppings, quartz veins, and an area associated with Texas
Blue Topaz, the State Gemstone.40 And, as discussed above, Harkey Ranch is recognized as a
Texas Century Ranch/Family Land Heritage Ranch.41 On a site-specific level, Route 894 avoids
that historic ranch and the detrimental impact that placement of an extremely high-voltage
transmission line would have on it.
     iv.           Environmental integrity
        Route 894 is one of the strongest performing routes with respect to environmental
integrity.42 It includes 291 stream crossings, which is tied with Route 891 for lowest among the
Routes of Interest.43 Route 894 also has only 1.97 miles of potential wetlands, second lowest
among the Routes of Interest, behind Route 891 by only 0.03 miles.44 Route 894 crosses 42.52
miles of riparian areas, which is materially lower than Routes of Interest 487, 392, and 410 and
comparable to Route 891.45 As discussed above Route 894 crosses no park or recreational area,
has no park or recreational area within 1,000 feet.46 Therefore, on matters of environmental
sensitivity, Route 894 is among the best performing routes compared with the other Routes of
Interest.

    B. Any route selected should exclude Links K42 and L1.

       Among the Routes of Interest, only Route 572 and CCG include Link K42, and none of
them include Link L1.47 Multiple feasible routes therefore avoid both links while performing as
well as or better than the routes that include Link K42 as to cost, habitable structures,
cultural/historical metrics, and stream crossings. Route 894 is the strongest of those and avoids
both Link L1 and Link K42 while outperforming the Routes of Interest that include Link K42, as
discussed herein.
       Link K42 alone or in combination with Link L1 would threaten safe aircraft operations at
the Ranch's two runways and nearby residences. It would place a large transmission-line obstacle
complex in a location that materially interferes with safe use of the Ranch runways. Selection of a
route including both Link K42 and Link L1 creates a deadly right angle or box canyon hazard.48
       Link L1 would materially impair headquarters and agricultural infrastructure, irreparably
harm historical, aesthetic, geological, and ecological resources, and impose avoidable easement
and damage costs where less harmful and less expensive routing options exist.49 Therefore, routes
avoiding Link L1 and Link K42 should be preferred.50
       The Commission should not require Texans to bear severe, avoidable impacts to their land
and property when, under the applicable routing criteria, there is a more efficient and less harmful
route. Route 894 satisfies the Project need, remains viable and constructible, and best balances the
statutory and Commission rule criteria while avoiding or significantly diminishing such
detrimental impacts. Harkey Ranch does not oppose the Project; however, given the profoundly
destructive impact that the Project would have if sited along or within the Harkey Ranch, any
selected route should therefore exclude Link K42 and Link L1.

                                          III.     CONCLUSION

       For the reasons stated above, Harkey Ranch respectfully requests that the Administrative
Law Judges recommend, and the Commission approve, selection of Route 894 for the Project.
Route 894 best balances the statutory factors in PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and the rule criteria in 16

                                              II.      ARGUMENT

    A. After balancing all factors specified by statute and PUCT rules, Route 894 best
       satisfies the routing criteria set forth in PURA and in Commission rules.

         1.   Factors Required to be Considered

          PURA § 37.056(c) specifies particular factors the Commission must consider when
granting or denying a CCN. The Commission is directed to consider the adequacy of existing
service, the need for additional service, the effect of granting the certificate on the applicant and
other utilities serving the proximate area, and other factors including community values,
recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, and environmental integrity.
Additionally, the Commission' s Substantive Rules at 16 Tex. Admin. Code ("TAC") §
25.101(b)(3)(B) articulate with more specificity required consideration of engineering constraints,
costs, use or paralleling of existing compatible rights-of-way, paralleling of apparent property
boundaries or other natural or cultural features, moderation of impact on the affected community
and landowners, and the Commission's policy of prudent avoidance.

         2. The Route best balancing the factors set out in statute and rule should be selected.

        Neither statute nor rule direct any single metric be controlling in the selection of a route on
which a transmission line will be placed. Nor does the Legislature assign values for any of the
designated factors to be weighed against each other. Rather, the Commission is called to evaluate
and weigh the routing criteria holistically. As former Chairman Barry Smitherman testified, "It' s
not a math question. It' s a balancing of factors."10

         In recommending Route 894, the record evidence shows that the Applicants assessed the
alternatives in just that way.11

      i.            Communitv Values, Prudent Avoidance, Habitable Structures
           Evaluation of route selection for a transmission line such as the one at issue in this
proceeding requires consideration ofvalues and resources essential to a local community.25 Under
16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), a transmission line must be routed to the extent reasonable to moderate
the impact on the affected community and landowners unless grid reliability and security dictate
otherwise. It follows, then, that the route selected should minimize disruption to land use, industry,
and the local residents and their way of life.

           Route 894 best serves community values and adheres to the Commission's policy of
prudent avoidance because it minimizes direct residential exposure. Route 894 has only 85
habitable structures within 500 feet of the route centerline, which is the fewest of the eight Routes
of Interest.26 By comparison, Route 894 includes 11 fewer habitable structures than Route 487,20
fewer than Route 296 and CCG, 22 fewer than Route 572,23 fewer than Route 891, and 51 fewer

     B. Any route selected should exclude Links K42 and Ll.

        Among the Routes of Interest, only Route 572 and CCG include Link K42, and none of
them include Link Ll.47 Multiple feasible routes therefore avoid both links while performing as
well as or better than the routes that include Link K42 as to cost, habitable structures,
cultural/historical metrics, and stream crossings. Route 894 is the strongest of those and avoids
both Link Ll and Link K42 while outperforming the Routes of Interest that include Link K42, as
discussed herein.
        Link K42 alone or in combination with Link L1 would threaten safe aircraft operations at
the Ranch's two runways and nearby residences. It would place a large transmission-line obstacle
complex in a location that materially interferes with safe use of the Ranch runways. Selection of a
route including both Link K42 and Link Ll creates a deadly right angle or box canyon hazard.48
        Link L1 would materially impair headquarters and agricultural infrastructure, irreparably
harm historical, aesthetic, geological, and ecological resources, and impose avoidable easement
and damage costs where less harmful and less expensive routing options exist.49 Therefore, routes
avoiding Link Ll and Link K42 should be preferred. 50
        The Commission should not require Texans to bear severe, avoidable impacts to their land
and property when, under the applicable routing criteria, there is a more efficient and less harmful
route. Route 894 satisfies the Proj ect need, remains viable and constructible, and best balances the
statutory and Commission rule criteria while avoiding or significantly diminishing such
detrimental impacts. Harkey Ranch does not oppose the Project; however, given the profoundly
destructive impact that the Proj ect would have if sited along or within the Harkey Ranch, any
selected route should therefore exclude Link K42 and Link Ll.
